title: They fade, sad phantoms: all is gone. Agendath is a waste land, a home of screechowls and the sandblind upupa. Netaim, the golden, is no more. And on the highway of the clouds they come, muttering thunder of rebellion, the ghosts of beasts.
html_source:
The antecedent noun to the pronoun “they” could also be more “souls,” or it could be “stars.” “Twilight phantoms” above already seems to fall back on “stars,” but the mention of “structure, haunches, necks, and skulls points to the mare and her fillyfoal. That the pronoun "she” wants to point back to “soul,” especially inasmuch as the soul is used repeatedly in Ulysses, Portrait of the Artist, and in classical literature generally using the feminine gender, makes it hard to argue that we are not talking about a soul (of either gender) and its mother (or father if we’re using “feminine” as gender-neutral in reference to souls).

The section suggesting the style of De Quincy notwithstanding , to this point it seems to bear a strong, but satirical, correlation to Wordsworth’s Ode: Imitations of Immortality, notably, its fifth stanza, especially if we’re talking about souls here. To begin with, the stanza begins with the words “Our birth.” The birth process, Mrs. Purefoy giving birth as the chapter’s setting, the theme of the disinclination of Irish youth in contributing to the volume of Irish births, all leave a strong link. Wordsworth’s “Soul that rises with us,” he describes as, “our life’s Star points to a "scattered … perennial dew of stars here”. Forms of the word “cloud” are used three times in Joyce’s passage. Wordsworth claims that it is “trailing clouds of glory [that we do] come/From God, who is our home.” The Ode’s serene soul “cometh from afar,"lying on its cloud, forgetting and asleep. Joyce’s "souls” come on a misty highway “muttering thunder of rebellion, the ghosts of beasts.” It must be noted that De Quincy was very closely associated with Wordsworth, lived near him in the Lake District, and wrote a series of reminiscences of the great poet.

Agendath Nataim is a very important symbol in Ulysses; the reference appears thirteen separate times in the novel as a promised land, despite the disparagement it appears to receive in this instance – another reason I believe the insolence of the souls in the passage is also meant as irony. The ad he had seen earlier in the day calling on European Jews like himself to become part of the cultivation of Palestine, a restoration of Zion, and the poorly drafted, disjointed, contradiction-laden notice brings to Bloom’s mind the fecklessness of the Celtic revivalist movement in resolving the persistent problems of identity for Ireland. It is of Ireland and not Palestine of which Joyce is speaking here as “a waste land, a home of screechowls and the sandblind upupa,” (a weak-sighted bird that lines its nest with human excrement).
